meta.title: Who really said "Methinks the lady doth protest too much"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: It's genuinely Shakespeare — Gertrude in Hamlet 3.2 — but misquoted. He wrote "The lady doth protest too much, methinks," with "methinks" last.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Methinks the lady doth protest too much'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely from Shakespeare's Hamlet, but reordered. The original line puts "methinks" at the end: "The lady doth protest too much, methinks."

answer.label: Shakespeare — but misquoted
answer.sourceLine: The thought and the words are Shakespeare’s — Queen Gertrude says this in Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 2, watching the play-within-the-play. But he wrote “The lady doth protest too much, methinks,” with “methinks” at the end. The popular “Methinks the lady doth protest too much” moves it to the front — a rearrangement that appears in no early text of the play.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
HAMLET: Madam, how like you this play?
QUEEN GERTRUDE: The lady doth protest too much, methinks.
HAMLET: O, but she’ll keep her word.
trail: The line is Queen Gertrude’s in Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 2 ↗, spoken as she watches the Player Queen’s over-emphatic vows — and it ends on the word “methinks.”
Wikipedia’s article, titled with the original word order, notes that “Methinks the lady doth protest too much” is a common rearrangement ↗ that moves “methinks” to the front.
Here “protest” carries its older sense of ‘vow’ or ‘declare’ ↗, not the modern ‘object’ — so Gertrude is saying the vows are too insistent to be sincere.
source.excerptNote: Note the order: Shakespeare ends the line on “methinks.” Editions vary between “doth protest” (Second Quarto) and “protests” (First Folio), but every early text keeps “methinks” last.
source.rightsNote: Hamlet was first printed between 1603 and 1623, so both the play and this line are firmly in the public domain in the United States. Only particular modern editorial texts or annotations could carry their own rights.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare wrote Hamlet around 1600–1601; it was printed in quarto in 1603 and 1604 and in the First Folio of 1623. The line belongs to Queen Gertrude, who watches a staged play murder Hamlet has arranged to catch his uncle’s conscience. In Shakespeare’s English protest meant to vow or declare — Gertrude means the Player Queen’s vows of fidelity are too emphatic to be believed, not that she is ‘objecting.’

misattribution.heading: What's really going on
misattribution.intro: The credit to Shakespeare is correct — this is one of the rare ‘famous quotes’ that really is from the play it’s pinned to. What’s wrong is the wording and, often, the meaning.

items.why: Shakespeare put “methinks” last: “The lady doth protest too much, methinks” ↗. Fronting it is a modern rearrangement found in no early quarto or folio.
Today the phrase implies a strong denial betrays guilt. In Shakespeare’s English ‘protest’ meant to vow or declare ↗ — Gertrude means the Player Queen’s promises are too emphatic to trust.

misattribution.truthLine: It’s genuinely from Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 2 ↗, spoken by Gertrude — but Shakespeare wrote “The lady doth protest too much, methinks,” with “methinks” at the end.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The play-within-a-play, the ‘Mousetrap,’ is Hamlet’s trap for his uncle Claudius: a staged re-enactment of the murder, watched for a flinch of guilt. Gertrude’s aside about the Player Queen’s vows — too loud, too insistent — is a small line that has outgrown the scene.

Detached from the stage, it became a universal put-down for anyone whose loud denials seem to give the game away. The reordered, ‘methinks’-first version simply flows better as a stand-alone quip, which is likely why it, rather than the original, is the one people repeat.
context.pull: Genuinely Shakespeare — just not in that order.
